title: Loan-to-value
body: LTV is the loan divided by the lower of the price or the appraised value. A higher LTV means more risk for the lender, so it can mean higher rates or mortgage insurance.
example: A Henderson buyer borrows $360,000 on a $400,000 home: 90% LTV.
hook: LTV: loan over value, lower value wins.

title: Points
body: A point is 1% of the loan amount, not the price. Discount points are prepaid interest that lowers the rate. More points up front usually means a lower payment over time.
example: Two points on a $300,000 Reno loan cost $6,000.
hook: A point is 1% of the loan, not the price.

title: Mortgage insurance and equity
body: Conventional loans above 80% LTV usually need PMI, which protects the lender. FHA loans have MIP instead. Equity is value minus debt, and it grows as you pay down the loan and as value rises.
example: A Las Vegas home worth $450,000 with a $300,000 loan has $150,000 in equity.

title: Government-backed loans
body: FHA insures loans and allows low down payments. VA guarantees loans for eligible veterans, often with no money down. USDA backs rural loans. None of these agencies normally lend the money themselves; approved lenders do.
example: A Nellis Air Force Base airman buys a North Las Vegas home with a VA loan and no down payment.
hook: FHA insures, VA guarantees, approved lenders lend.

title: How payments behave
body: A fixed-rate loan keeps the same rate. An ARM's rate moves with an index plus a margin, within caps. A balloon loan leaves a big final payment. A reverse mortgage pays older owners from their equity.
example: A Reno buyer takes a 5/1 ARM: fixed for five years, then adjusting yearly.

title: Creative financing
body: In seller financing, the seller carries back a note: a purchase money mortgage. A blanket loan covers several parcels. A wraparound includes an existing loan inside a new one.
example: A Pahrump developer's blanket loan covers 20 lots, with a release clause as each lot sells.
hook: Blanket covers many. Wrap covers one inside another.

title: Note and security instrument
body: The promissory note is the promise to pay. The mortgage or deed of trust pledges the property as security. A deed of trust has three parties: trustor (borrower), trustee, and beneficiary (lender).
example: Most Nevada home loans use a deed of trust, so a trustee can sell the property in a nonjudicial foreclosure.
hook: The note is the debt. The deed of trust is the collateral.

title: Key loan clauses
body: An acceleration clause makes the whole balance due on default. An alienation (due-on-sale) clause makes it due on transfer. A prepayment penalty charges for paying off early. Subordination changes lien priority.
example: A Henderson seller deeds the home to a buyer without paying off the loan. The lender invokes due-on-sale.
hook: Accelerate on default. Alienate on sale.

title: Assumption vs. subject to
body: A buyer who assumes a loan becomes personally liable, usually with lender approval. A buyer who takes subject to the loan isn't personally liable; the seller stays liable. Lien theory leaves title with the borrower; title theory gives it to the lender or trustee.
example: A Reno buyer assumes the seller's FHA loan with lender approval.
hook: Assume it, own the debt. Subject to it, don't.

title: From prequal to approval
body: Prequalification is a quick estimate from what the borrower says. Preapproval means the lender checked credit and documents. Underwriting then confirms the borrower's ability to repay and the property's value.
example: A Las Vegas listing agent prefers offers with a preapproval letter over a prequalification.
hook: Prequal is a guess. Preapproval is checked.

title: Qualifying ratios
body: Lenders compare monthly debts to gross monthly income. The front-end ratio counts housing costs; the back-end ratio counts all debts. Traditional conventional guidelines were about 28% and 36%, though programs vary.
example: A Henderson borrower earns $8,000 a month. 28% allows a $2,240 housing payment.

title: The secondary market
body: Lenders make loans in the primary market, then sell them in the secondary market to get more money to lend. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy conventional loans. Ginnie Mae guarantees securities backed by FHA and VA loans.
example: A Reno credit union sells its 30-year loans to Fannie Mae and lends the money again.
hook: Primary makes it. Secondary buys it.

title: Truth in Lending
body: TILA and Regulation Z require clear disclosure of credit costs, including the APR. In ads, trigger terms, like the down payment or monthly payment, require full disclosure of the terms.
example: A Las Vegas ad that says "only $1,900 a month" must also show the APR and other required terms.
hook: Say a number, show them all.

title: RESPA and TRID
body: RESPA bans kickbacks for referrals of settlement services. Under TRID, borrowers get a Loan Estimate within 3 business days of applying and a Closing Disclosure at least 3 business days before closing.
example: A Henderson buyer gets the Closing Disclosure on Monday, so consummation can't happen until Thursday.
hook: Three days to estimate, three days before close.

title: Fair lending and fraud
body: ECOA bans credit discrimination, including by age, marital status, and receipt of public assistance. Mortgage fraud includes lying about income or occupancy. Predatory lending strips equity through unfair loans.
example: A Reno lender can't deny a qualified applicant because their income comes from public assistance.
hook: ECOA adds age, marriage, and assistance.
